## Nursing Workforce Data in the MOH Statistical Yearbook

Based on the available context, the following nursing workforce data is present in the MOH Statistical Yearbook (1437H), broken down by **specialisation status** (Specialised [S] vs. Non-Specialised [NS]) and **sex** [4]:

| Category | Sex | Specialised (S) | Non-Specialised (NS) | Total |
|----------|-----|----------------:|---------------------:|------:|
| Nurses | Male | 551 | 3,232 | 3,783 |
| Nurses | Female | 835 | 17,528 | 18,363 |
| **Nurses Total** | | **1,386** | **20,760** | **22,146** |

> **Source:** MOH Statistical Yearbook 1437H, Table 2-32 [4]

---

### Notes:
- The data distinguishes between **specialised** and **non-specialised** nurses for both male and female categories.
- The table also includes data for **Physicians** and **Allied Health Personnel**, but the specific nursing figures above represent the nurses category exclusively.
- I could not find more recent nursing-specific workforce breakdowns in the current context. The **MOH Statistical Yearbook 2023** is referenced across several sources [1][2][3][5] as the most current publication, but its specific nursing workforce tables are **not available in the provided context**. For the latest figures, the full yearbook is accessible at: [https://www.moh.gov.sa/en/Ministry/Statistics/book/Pages/default.aspx](https://www.moh.gov.sa/en/Ministry/Statistics/book/Pages/default.aspx)
per_question.reference: The MOH Statistical Yearbook provides nursing workforce data including the number of nursing staff and midwives across all health regions and sectors (Ministry of Health, other governmental, private). Data is broken down by nationality (Saudi vs non-Saudi) and covers multiple years for trend analysis. The yearbook also tracks allied health personnel separately.

## Health Resources Statistics in the MOH Statistical Yearbook

Based on the available context, the MOH Statistical Yearbook covers the following types of health resources statistics:

### Chapter II: Health Resources

The yearbook includes detailed tables covering:

- **Administrative Personnel and Workers** in the Ministry of Health, broken down by sex and nationality [4]
- **Health Manpower** in MOH Headquarters and Regional Health Directorates, categorised by:
  - Category
  - Sex
  - Nationality
  - Region [4]
- **MOH Hospitals and Beds by Region**, including data across the last five years [4]
- **MOH Hospitals and Beds by Region and Speciality** [4]
- **MOH Hospitals by Bed Capacity and Region** [4]
- **Beds at MOH Hospitals by Region and Speciality** [4]
- **Health Manpower in MOH Hospitals by Nationality**, across the last five years [4]
- **Health Manpower in MOH Hospitals by Region, Category, Sex, and Nationality** [4]
- **Physicians and Dentists in MOH Hospitals**, broken down by speciality, professional category, and region [4]
- **Primary Health Care Centers in MOH by Region**, including data across the last five years [4]

---

> **Note:** The above structure is drawn from the 2018 edition of the Statistical Yearbook (1439H/2018G) as reflected in the available context [4]. The yearbook is published annually and the most recent edition cited is the **Statistical Yearbook 2023**, available from the MOH website [1][2][3], though the detailed chapter breakdown for that edition is not fully visible in the current context.
per_question.reference: The MOH Statistical Yearbook covers health resources including the number of hospitals, hospital beds, primary healthcare centers, and healthcare personnel such as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and allied health workers. Statistics are broken down by health region and by nationality (Saudi vs non-Saudi).

# MOH Health Services and Emergency Facilities During the Hajj Season

Based on the available context from MOH Statistical Yearbooks, the Ministry of Health provides a comprehensive range of health services and facilities during the Hajj season. The following is drawn from the most recent available source (2023) and corroborated by earlier yearbooks.

---

## 1. Health Facilities
MOH deploys both **permanent and seasonal health facilities** throughout the Hajj season. This includes fixed hospitals and health centers as well as temporary facilities set up specifically for the season. [1][2][3]

---

## 2. Entry Point Preventive Care
**Preventive health surveillance centers** are stationed at all **entry points** (ports of entry) to monitor arriving pilgrims, conducting health screening and control activities to prevent the spread of communicable diseases. [1][2][3]

---

## 3. Dedicated Manpower
The MOH assigns **dedicated manpower** exclusively for the Hajj season, separate from the regular health workforce, to manage the surge in healthcare demand. [1][2][3]

---

## 4. Clinical and Emergency Services
According to the index tables of the MOH Statistical Yearbooks [2][3][5], the following specific clinical and emergency services are documented as being provided to pilgrims during the Hajj season:

| Service | Reference Table |
|---|---|
| Visits to Primary Health Care Centers (PHCs) | Table 5-5 |
| Emergency Room (ER) visits at hospitals | Table 5-6 |
| Outpatient Department (OPD) visits at hospitals | Table 5-7 |
| Hospital admissions/inpatient care | Table 5-8 |
| Heat exhaustion case management | Table 5-9 |
| Heat stroke case management | Table 5-10 |
| Cardiac catheterization procedures | Table 5-11 |
| Open heart surgeries | Table 5-12 |
| Renal (haemodialysis) dialysis sessions | Table 5-13 |
| Endoscopy procedures | Table 5-14 |
| Maternity/delivery services | Table 5-15 |
| Pilgrim mortality monitoring | Table 5-16 |

[2][3]

---

## 5. Pilgrim Monitoring
MOH also tracks and monitors **pilgrims from inside and outside the Kingdom**, covering the last ten years of data, to plan and scale services accordingly. [2][3][5]

---

> **Note:** The context provides the **structure and categories** of services documented in the MOH Statistical Yearbooks (2018–2023). The specific numerical data within each of these service categories is not included in the provided context. For exact figures, please refer directly to the respective tables in the MOH Statistical Yearbook 2023 [1].
per_question.reference: Saudi Arabia provides comprehensive health services during Hajj season including preventive care at entry points, primary care at health centers, emergency room departments at hospitals in Makkah and Madinah, and specialized services such as cardiac catheterization and open heart surgery for pilgrims. The MOH yearbook dedicates a full chapter to Hajj health services statistics covering the last five years.

# Standards and Requirements for Urgent Care Centers (UCCs) — MOH Policy

Based on the available MOH policy document (*UrgentCare\_Center\_Standard\_Policy*), the following standards and requirements are outlined:

---

## 1. Purpose and Objectives

The MOH policy document aims to achieve the following [2][5]:

- **1.1.1** Standardize UCC practice across the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
- **1.1.2** Provide practical recommendations on preparing and operating UCCs.
- **1.1.3** Provide clear UCC pathways, structures, policies, guidelines, essential checklists, and **mandatory competencies** for all staff working in UCCs.
- **1.1.4** Define **quality control measures** for evaluating the performance of UCCs.
- **1.1.5** Emphasize that the ideal standard of UCCs is a **stand-alone model**, either **Level 1 or Level 2**, based on MOH regulation.

---

## 2. Operational & Design Requirements

- The design of a UCC should prioritize **efficient patient flow, accessibility**, and integration of necessary medical facilities and technologies to provide rapid, effective treatment in a safe and patient-friendly environment, in a model of stand-alone UCCs according to MOH regulation. [4]
- All UCCs must have a **visual nurse** who visually assesses the severity of a patient's illness upon arrival. [3]
- The **Urgent Care Service Line Lead** (Emergency Service Lead in the MOH Cluster) is responsible for overseeing:
  - Delivery and quality of medical services
  - Coordination of patient care
  - Operational efficiency and compliance with healthcare standards within their designated service line [3]

---

## 3. Reference Standards

The policy references the following accreditation and standards bodies [1]:

- **National Hospital Standards** — Saudi Central Board for Accreditation of Healthcare Institutions (CBAHI)
- **Joint Commission International (JCI)** Accreditation Standards for Hospitals
- **American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP)**
- **National Urgent Care Center Accreditation**
- MOH *Guide to Excellence in Primary Health Care Centers* (2009)

---

> **Note:** The context available covers key sections of the policy. For the complete technical specifications, staffing competencies, and full operational checklists, the full MOH *UrgentCare\_Center\_Standard\_Policy* document should be consulted directly.
per_question.reference: The MOH Urgent Care Center Standard Policy (effective January 2025) aims to standardize Urgent Care Center (UCC) practice across Saudi Arabia and provide practical guidance. Stand-alone UCCs operate according to MOH regulation. The Urgent Care Service Line Lead (Emergency Service Lead in the MOH Cluster) oversees delivery and quality of medical services, coordinates patient care, and ensures operational standards. UCC design should prioritize efficient patient flow, accessibility, and the integration of necessary medical facilities and technologies to provide rapid, effective treatment.

## CTAS and Visual Nurse Roles in MOH Urgent Care Centers

### The Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS)

According to MOH policy, the **CTAS** is defined as *"a tool used both nationally and internationally"* to allow healthcare centers and their staff to prioritize patient care requirements [3]. It operates across **five acuity levels** that classify patients based on the severity of their condition [5].

All patients presenting to Urgent Care Centers (UCCs) **must be assessed by a triage nurse using the CTAS**, regardless of their eligibility status. The scale helps healthcare professionals determine the urgency of a patient's need for medical treatment [4].

---

### The Visual Nurse's Role in Initial Triage

The visual nurse plays a critical frontline role in the triage process, as outlined below [1][2]:

- **Initial Assessment:** The visual nurse is the **first to assess all patients** entering the center.
- **Visual Screening:** They are responsible for **visually assessing patients as they arrive**, to quickly gauge the severity of their condition. This informal, immediate assessment is designed to prioritize patients for further evaluation and treatment — particularly in busy settings where triage efficiency is crucial.
- **Critical Case Escalation:** If the visual nurse detects any **concerning cases** — such as a patient with **chest pain or shortness of breath** — they must:
  - Directly send the patient to the **critical care area**
  - Connect the patient to a **cardiac monitor**
  - **Measure vital signs**
  - **Obtain an ECG** if indicated
  - **Inform the physician without delay**

- **Handover to Reception:** Following the visual nursing process, the patient is then directed to **reception for registration** [2].

---

> ⚠️ *This information is drawn from the MOH Urgent Care Center Standard Policy. It is intended for informational purposes only and does not constitute clinical or medical advice.*
per_question.reference: The MOH Urgent Care Center Standard Policy specifies that UCCs use the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) with five acuity levels to help healthcare centers and their staff prioritize patient care requirements. A visual nurse performs initial triage at the UCC. If the visual nurse detects any concerning cases such as a patient with chest pain or shortness of breath, the patient is sent directly to the critical care area. Patient documentation must include personal information, date and time of arrival, arrival mode, vital signs, and chief complaint.

## توزيع إحصاءات الأطباء وأطباء الأسنان على القطاعات الصحية

استناداً إلى أحدث البيانات المتاحة من الكتاب الإحصائي لوزارة الصحة لعام 2022م، يُوزَّع الأطباء وأطباء الأسنان على ثلاثة قطاعات رئيسية على النحو الآتي: [2]

---

### الجدول: توزيع الأطباء وأطباء الأسنان حسب القطاع الصحي، 2022م

| القطاع | الفئة | العدد | نسبة السعوديين (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **وزارة الصحة** | أطباء بشريون | 55,487 | 47.5% |
| | أطباء أسنان | 7,153 | 92.2% |
| | **إجمالي الأطباء** | **62,640** | **52.6%** |
| **الجهات الحكومية الأخرى** | أطباء بشريون | 19,644 | 60.1% |
| | أطباء أسنان | 1,853 | 83.2% |
| | **إجمالي الأطباء** | **21,497** | **62.1%** |
| **القطاع الخاص** | أطباء بشريون | 30,201 | 16.1% |
| | أطباء أسنان | 14,891 | 31.2% |
| | **إجمالي الأطباء** | **45,092** | **21.1%** |
| **المجموع الكلي** | أطباء بشريون | 105,332 | 40.8% |
| | أطباء أسنان | 23,897 | 53.5% |
| | **إجمالي الأطباء** | **129,229** | **43.2%** |

---

### أبرز الملاحظات:

- **وزارة الصحة** تستأثر بالحصة الأكبر من الأطباء بإجمالي **62,640** طبيباً وطبيب أسنان، أي ما يعادل نحو **48.5%** من إجمالي الأطباء في المملكة. [2]
- **القطاع الخاص** يحتل المرتبة الثانية بـ **45,092** طبيباً وطبيب أسنان، وتتميز نسبة السعوديين فيه بكونها الأدنى بين القطاعات (**21.1%**). [2]
- **الجهات الحكومية الأخرى** (كالجامعات والمستشفيات العسكرية وغيرها) تضم **21,497** طبيباً وطبيب أسنان. [2]
- تُسجَّل أعلى نسبة سعودة في فئة **أطباء الأسنان بوزارة الصحة** إذ بلغت **92.2%** عام 2022م. [2]

---

> **ملاحظة منهجية:** يُصنِّف الكتاب الإحصائي هذه البيانات ضمن **الجدول 2-4** الذي يعرض إحصاءات القوى العاملة الصحية للسنوات الخمس الأخيرة (2018–2022م)، مما يتيح تتبع الاتجاهات الزمنية لكل قطاع. [2]
